extracted.intended_audience: researchers, scientometricians, research-evaluation policymakers, and science-communication scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical criteria for evaluating the use of written-press attention (newspapers and magazines) as evidence or proxy of the societal impact of university research, including methodological notes for data collection and caveats for integration into evaluation systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written press attention as a pathway to SIUR
rubrics_metrics.description: Written media like newspapers and magazines seem a more relevant pathway to effectuate societal impact due to their recognition in qualitative assessment tools and their broad, societal reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mainstream print media attention as a potential modality of societal impact (SIUR), but do not assume that any mention equals a significant or causal contribution; consider the type and substance of the coverage before attributing impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altmetrics limitations for measuring SIUR
rubrics_metrics.description: Altmetrics rely on social media and are susceptible to manipulation and mostly reflect circulation among niche audiences rather than broad societal reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when using altmetrics as evidence of societal impact: account for academic spamming, audience composition (often other academics), and the limited convergent validity with richer qualitative impact measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate types of media attention (substantial vs. cursory vs. authored)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media attention is heterogeneous: only 7.2% of articles involved substantial, in-depth discussion of research; 53.5% involved short expert explanations (a few sentences); and a subset are opinion pieces/columns authored by researchers (often professors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify and weight mentions by type—give greater evidential weight to sustained, research-based discussion or authored pieces explaining methods/results, and treat brief expert quotes as weak indicators of SIUR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness vs proactivity of researcher presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence in the written press is predominantly a responsive phenomenon: 87.1% of articles were authored by journalists/editors, indicating journalists act as gatekeepers who determine when, why and how scholars are presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating media-derived impact, distinguish researcher-initiated outreach (proactive communication, press releases, authored pieces) from journalist-driven, responsive appearances; proactive instances may better demonstrate intentional science communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject- or discipline-dependence of media opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Media attention is highly subject-dependent: certain disciplines (e.g., political science in election years) offer easier pathways to popularization than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust expectations and comparisons across disciplines; do not treat raw media-mention counts as comparable across fields with differing topicality to mainstream news cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status-dependence and concentration of media visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Media appearance is strongly status-dependent and skewed: a small number of high-status researchers (e.g., eight male professors) accounted for almost half of media mentions; professors were much more likely to be mentioned than predocs/postdocs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for status bias (Matthew effects) when using press mentions in evaluation to avoid privileging established scholars and exacerbating inequality; consider normalizing or contextualizing counts by career stage or other indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender disparities in media representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Male social scientists featured considerably more often (63.2%) than female scientists (36.8%), with disparities most pronounced at professorial levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When incorporating media presence into assessment, adjust for gender imbalances or report gender-disaggregated metrics to avoid reinforcing existing underrepresentation of women in media visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization and celebrity (visibility) effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalization of science and the rise of 'public intellectuals' or 'celebrity scientists' create self-reinforcing dynamics where prior visibility leads to further media presence, sometimes irrespective of specific research contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate celebrity or personal fame with research impact; include checks that media attention reflects research-based contributions rather than general public notoriety or commentary on unrelated issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication and incidence vs reach due to media concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: High media concentration and conglomerate ownership can cause content to migrate across multiple titles, inflating the apparent incidence of mentions without proportionally increasing unique reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer measures of reach/audience or unique placements over raw article counts; deduplicate syndicated content and account for ownership structures when estimating societal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to filter non-research mentions and namesakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all press mentions of a researcher relate to their university research (e.g., political mandates); namesakes can generate false positives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement filtering rules: exclude impertinent documents, verify whether mentions concern research activities, disambiguate namesakes, and remove coverage unrelated to research to avoid inflating SIUR indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press mentions may originate from press releases or publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Written-press coverage can be traced to press releases or productive publications, but many media appearances do not cite specific scholarly publications and may instead personalize research insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, trace mentions back to originating materials (press releases, publications) and document whether the coverage accurately represents research findings; prefer instances with clear linkage to scholarly outputs for SIUR claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citable nature of written media vs social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers and magazines are largely disambiguated and citable, making them plausible candidates for inclusion in evaluation instruments compared to social media signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While citable, treat press mentions as one type of evidence and combine with qualitative explanation of contribution; do not rely solely on citable status to claim societal impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer qualitative, case-based evidence for SIUR (impact cases/SIAMPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative approaches (e.g., REF impact cases, SIAMPI productive interactions) habitually admit non-scholarly communication as a modality of potential SIUR, viewing clear non-scholarly communication as a precondition for societal impact but not proof of causal effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement quantitative media indicators with qualitative narratives and evidence that demonstrate how media presence contributed to societal outcomes; use mixed methods rather than pure counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against simplistic quantitative integration into evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplistic integrations of written-press objects into research assessment schemes risk disproportionately disadvantaging early career researchers and exasperating existing inequalities, and may misrepresent true SIUR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid naively adding press-mention counts to evaluation scores; if included, apply normalization, weighting by substance, and safeguards to mitigate perverse incentives and inequitable effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure substance of contribution — research-based public interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Only a minority of media appearances amount to demonstrable research-based public interventions or knowledge transfers; many contributions are descriptive or used to reinforce journalists' arguments rather than present investigative context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require evidence that a media appearance communicated research methods, results, or led to identifiable societal outcomes before crediting it as SIUR; distinguish descriptive expert quotes from interventions with traceable influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal context and atypical periods affect media-based indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain periods (e.g., the COVID-19 pandemic years) produce atypical media dynamics that distort typical patterns of media attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude or treat atypical time windows cautiously; use temporally demarcated datasets and justify period selection to avoid misinterpretation of spikes or troughs in media attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological exhaustiveness and institutional inclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: An exhaustive, temporally demarcated collection of written-press documents referencing researchers (using institutional databases like FRIS and media databases like GoPress), combined with institution-based inclusion criteria, supports robust analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt clear inclusion rules (which institutions/disciplines/languages to include), document searching and disambiguation procedures, and report coding schemas (e.g., coding for type of media attention) to ensure replicability and validity.
